title: How big a sensor can a K-frame burst of a small sensor stand in for?
lede: inverting the burst break-even formula: the largest sensor-area ratio a K-frame burst matches runs from √K in the dark to K in bright light, so 8 frames at 3 e⁻ read noise match a 4×-area frame from 4.5 e⁻ per pixel per frame, a 6× frame from 21 e⁻ and never an 8× frame; Monte Carlo agrees to 1% in variance at 18 settings. Model only, swept ranges not sourced to a device
summary: sensing-burst gave the break-even frame count N* = A2(e + r2)/(A e + r2) for a burst to match one frame from a sensor with A times the pixel area. This project solves it for A: the largest matched ratio is the positive root of (e + r2)A2 − K e A − K r2 = 0, between √K (read-noise limited) and K (shot-noise limited). Swept over 1 to 10,000 electrons per frame, read noise 1 to 10 electrons and K = 4, 8, 15: with 8 frames and 3 e− read noise a burst matches a 4× frame from 4.5 e− per pixel per frame and a 6× frame from 21 e−, and never an 8× frame; 15 frames match 12× from 3.6 e− (r = 1) to 358 e− (r = 10). A Monte Carlo of the Poisson-Gaussian model gives a variance ratio of 0.990 to 1.009 at 18 settings. Limits: it is the same model as sensing-burst (perfect registration, static scene, no clipping, dark current or fixed-pattern noise); the electron and read-noise ranges are swept, not taken from any device, because the one public sensor-data site found is all rights reserved.
